subject: physics
question_text: Which thermodynamic variable is defined by a) the zeroth law of thermodynamics b) the first law of thermodynamics?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 12 Very Short Answer Question 3 (printed p.124). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked against NCERT Class-11 Chapter 12: the zeroth law defines temperature, as the property equal for two systems in thermal equilibrium; the first law, ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW, defines internal energy as a state variable through the difference between heat supplied and work done.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: a) The zeroth law
lines: It is the property that is equal
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name temperature, and say it is equal for systems in equilibrium.
steps.why: Before the zeroth law, temperature is only a hotness felt by touch; the law gives it a working definition, as the property shared by any two systems in thermal equilibrium.
common_mistakes: Naming internal energy for the zeroth law instead of temperature.
Leaving out that temperature is defined through thermal equilibrium.

recall.must_convey: That the zeroth law defines temperature, as the property equal for two systems in thermal equilibrium.

steps.memory_tip: Zeroth comes first, and so does temperature — the zeroth law defines it.

steps.label: b) The first law
lines: It is a state variable — its
CHANGE is fixed by the first
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name internal energy, and give ΔQ = ΔU + ΔW.
steps.why: Heat and work both depend on the path taken, but their difference does not — that path-independent difference is what the first law identifies as internal energy, a state variable.
common_mistakes: Naming temperature again for the first law instead of internal energy.
Writing the first law without identifying which term is the newly defined variable.

recall.must_convey: That the first law defines internal energy, through ΔQ equals ΔU plus ΔW.
accept: delta Q equals delta U plus delta W

steps.memory_tip: First law, internal energy. Both are about the U in ΔU.

insider_note: Two different laws, two different variables — never answer both parts with the same word.
